chapter_theme: Pattinathar's Udarkootru Vannam tells the life of one body in four long units: the seed and blood that join in the womb and the child of five playing in the street dust; the youth of sixteen with his learning, his jewels and the women who take his capital, turning into the old man with a staff; the dying man fouled, speechless and signing with his hands as the four elements and the breath stop; and the corpse netted by Yama's messengers, washed, dressed, carried to the burning ground and burnt until not a handful of ash is left. Only the last word turns to the Lord: rule me, your servant, who trusts you now.
structure_note: The work is a single வண்ணம் in four stanzas, each a chain of participles that only closes in its last line (ஆகி விளையாடியே, ஆகியே, வரு நேரமே, ஆளுமே). The text is printed without word spaces, so the segmentation of several lines is the reader's. The stages are: conception to age five (808), sixteen to old age (809), decrepitude and death (810), funeral and prayer (811).

808.reading: A young woman and a man join; in the love that gives pleasure the senses blur and the seed flows and mixes with the welling blood; a drop half the size of a dew-drop enters the woman's belly and, like a lotus bud, becomes eyes, mouth, ears and hands and a form in which life grows; in the tenth month it leaves the womb and falls to earth, its day and star are noted, the women tend it, it kicks and drinks the nectar of the breast, grows from one sense to two, is kissed, crawls, lisps on the lap, is told 'come' and 'go', wears bells and a waist-cord, eats with the eaters, plays in the street dust with the boys, and reaches five years at play.
808.nuance: The conception is told physiologically (விந்து, சுரோணிதம்) and without disgust; the disgust is saved for 810 and 811. ஓரறிவு ஈரறிவு ஆகி வளர்ந்து uses the Tamil grading of living things by number of senses for the infant's growth. Two words are lost at the lacunae marked [***], one in the list of organs and one after மடந்[தை].

809.reading: At sixteen he has the teaching of a guru of lofty wisdom and the arts of Tamil to their shore, is praised as a waxing moon, dresses his hair with flowers that bees hum round, wears gold and gems and is bowed to by bards; women see him as Kama's form, crowd and throw their curved glances, and when they go like peacocks he runs after them, embraces, drinks the nectar of their lips and gives away the whole capital he had gathered; the hoarded wealth is lost to idleness, and calling this the pleasure and grief of Kama he parts from the youthful form; prosperity and youth change, the strong teeth fall, the two eyes darken, age ripens, grey hair and wrinkles come with wind, quarrel and anger, and a staff is in his red hand.
809.nuance: Learning and wealth are given to the youth only so that the women can strip them; the stanza does not call the women courtesans, but தேடிய மாமுதல் சேர வழங்கி (giving away all the capital he had sought) is the courtesan verses' plot. வாதவிரோதகுரோதம் can be read as the wind-disease of old age or as quarrelsomeness; தடி (staff) and நரைதிரை are the standard marks of age.

810.reading: A hunched back that comes and goes, a squatting walk like a monkey's, mind gone, ears numb, the mouth babbling without knowing, cough that will not let him sleep, throat and chest dried out, the cloth lost and shame gone, mocked by women and boys who ask whether the Kali age will respect such a one; faeces and urine come noisily and run down his legs and up; no clarity, speech stumbling, thought and heart shaken, firmness lost, grieving that there is no help; he sees that what Brahma wrote has come, that this is his end and his bond, that life in the world will not last, speaks of what he owes, and as his tongue falls asleep he speaks with his hands; gruel runs from the corner of his mouth, the four elements and the breath stop, and the heart falters: at that moment.
810.nuance: The stanza is the one place the dying man speaks: கண்டம் (the fatal hour) and தொந்தம் (the bond) are his own words, and கடன்முறை பேசும் (speaking of debts and duties) is the deathbed settling of accounts. பூதமு நாலு சுவாசமும் நின்று takes the body as four elements and the breath; the fifth, space, is not counted, perhaps because it does not depart. The chain ends mid-sentence (வரு நேரமே) and 811 begins the funeral.

811.reading: The teeth stand out like a crescent, the hair, matted locks and tufts grow long, the mind is dark and the form shows it; Yama's messengers come like a great mountain, cast their net and take the life; sons come bowed and weeping, the wife falls in his lap and wails that they fainted though they knew his time; neighbours say the old ones should see him, those standing by say put up the pandal and come beating the drum, asking that the corpse be burnt quickly; elders set many to work, some wash the corpse, they dress the stinking body in fine cloth, garlands and sandal and make a show of it, run crying 'lift it without breaking rank', the young sons bend and carry it, hurry to the burning ground, grieve that this is what human life is, cover it in firewood and set the fire; it burns, falls and breaks, the fat melts, the bones char and settle: a body that leaves not even a handful of ash. Rule me now, your servant who trusts you.
811.nuance: Only the final line (நம்பும் அடியேனை இனி ஆளுமே) addresses the Lord, so the whole four-stanza life is the ground of one prayer. மாழ்கினரே இவர் காலம் அறிந்து is hard: it may be the wife's cry that they swooned though they knew his time was near, or the neighbours' comment. ஓர் பிடி நீறும் இலாத உடம்பு (a body without even a handful of ash) is the price Pattinathar sets on the body, as Arunagirinathar does.

links.note: Both begin the body at the fall of the seed into the opened womb and have the faculties form from it: Tirumular counts the elements and faculties rising and hiding at the brow and crown; Pattinathar has the drop become eyes, mouth, ears and hands and a form in which life grows. Tirumular's is a tattva account, Pattinathar's a narrative.

The same opening of a life: Arunagirinathar's drop placed in the mother grows like a pea into flesh, blood and limbs through ten months to birth and first steps; Pattinathar's drop half a dew-drop mixes with the blood and becomes the organs, is born in the tenth month and lisps on the lap. Both poets tell the life only to show where it ends.

Both follow the man from the adorned women who clutch him to the ruin they leave: Arunagirinathar's wealth goes and stammering speech, a staff, disease and the sickbed follow; Pattinathar's youth gives the women all his capital and comes out with fallen teeth, dark eyes, grey hair and a staff in his hand.

The Naladiyar says those who delighted in fleeting youth later rise painfully on a staff, and that the wise renounced knowing grey hair would come; Pattinathar's stanza is that sentence drawn out, from the praised youth of sixteen to the staff in the red hand. The Naladiyar draws the lesson of early renunciation that Pattinathar leaves to the reader.

Both picture the moment of death as the body's closing and the kin's withdrawal: Tirumular's pandal comes apart, the nine gates shut together and the loving ones weep and go; Pattinathar's gruel runs from the mouth, the elements and breath stop and the heart falters, while in the next stanza sons and wife weep and the neighbours take over.

Pattinathar's own short verse to the body says that on the day mother, kin and wives let go and ask 'who are you, who am I', diseases come and settle in and only the mat stays a friend; the stanza shows that day in detail, with the mockery of women and boys, the fouled legs and the stumbling speech.

Both follow the corpse through the town's hands to the burning ground: Tirumular's town wails, renames the man a corpse, burns him and bathes and stops thinking of him; Pattinathar's neighbours call for the pandal and drum, the elders order the washing, the sons carry and burn it. Pattinathar adds that nothing is left, not even a handful of ash.

Sivavakkiyar's fine body, when the Arbiter calls, stinks and is carried only as far as the burning ground and handed to the keeper; Pattinathar's stinking body is dressed in silk and sandal for show and then carried fast to the burning ground. Sivavakkiyar sets the jealous lover before this end; Pattinathar sets the whole life before it.

Both close a life told from the womb with the same measure of the body: Arunagirinathar's is not worth a handful of ash after kin have wailed and the pyre has burnt; Pattinathar's burns, melts and chars until not even a handful of ash is left. The two works share the whole arc, drop, birth, women, staff, net of Death, pyre.

source_issues: 808: two lacunae marked [***] in the source, in the list of organs (செவிக[***]கைகளென்ற) and after மடந்[***]; the missing words are not recoverable from the text.
808: புகுந்து / ண்டு is broken across a line so that the word is split (புகுந்துண்டு).
809: செங்கையினி்லோர் carries a stray pulli (செங்கையினிலோர்); மங்கலசெங்கலசந்திகழ்கொங்கைம / ருவ splits a word across the line.
811: சிறுகுஞ்யும் is garbled, probably சிறுகுஞ்சியும் (small tufts of hair); தொங்கல்களபபணிந்து has a doubled consonant (களபம் அணிந்து).
The whole work is printed without word spaces, so segmentation is editorial throughout.
